newsitem.title: ITALY: MOTOR RACING-REFORMED PLAYBOY BERGER REACHES 200TH GRAND PRIX.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-REFORMED PLAYBOY BERGER REACHES 200TH GRAND PRIX.

text.p: After 14 years of incidents and accidents, reformed playboy Gerhard Berger is set to record his 200th Formula One start in Sunday's San Marino Grand Prix.
The 37-year-old Austrian, once dubbed the last of the playboys for his wild off-track antics during the early years of his career, has no intention of retiring.
Instead, he wants a 10th victory and a tilt at world drivers' title which has eluded him throughout a long and colourful career.

"I am still very fit and I feel in good condition, optimistic and motivated," he said. "Actually, it feels very strange for me to be in this kind of position because I just don't feel like I have done that many Grands Prix.
"I have no thought of retiring at all. I love this job. I cannot think of anything else I want to do. It is great for me and I am just enjoying every day the way I always have done."
For Berger, there is something appropriate in returning to Imola for his landmark 200th Grand Prix.
It was here that he saw his first race, won his first world championship podium finish and nearly lost his own life in a fireball accident in 1989.
His career has been highlighted by events at the picturesque circuit set in the rolling hillsides of Emilia Romagna and, as a result, he has poignant feelings each time he returns.
This year, those emotions are stronger than ever as he goes back to the Italian circuit where, in two spells, he raced in the red of Ferrari on what is widely regarded as their home Grand Prix track.

"Many things have happened to me there over the years, I could not come back without thinking of them," Berger recalled. "I saw my first Grand Prix at Imola, I had my first Formula One podium finish there (with Benetton in 1986), I had my worst accident there (with Ferrari, in 1989) and there was also the tragedy of Roland (Ratzenberger) and Ayrton's (Senna) deaths in 1994.
"So, I go back to Imola with a lot of feelings. It is emotional for me and it is special to go there for my 200th Grand Prix. Everything happens to me at Imola."

A reformed tearaway, who once revelled in danger and risk-taking as well as the company of beautiful women, Berger is now married and the father of three daughters. He admits he has found it difficult to reconcile his present settled life with a more colourful past.

But, he said, he felt the experiences at Imola in 1989, when he survived his own fireball crash at the Tamburello curve, and five years later in 1994, when Senna was killed at the same corner, have tempered his outlook on life.
"I learned to see things very differently," he said. "I used not to care. Now I do. Those big accidents changed the way I wanted to live.

"After 1989, I stopped taking so many risks and I thought about everything differently. After 1994, I nearly gave up racing altogether, but I decided I had to carry on. What else could I do? I love it. It is my life."
